title: Dutch report describes South Sea share prices during February trading
paraphrase: In Yale's published translation, a Dutch newspaper discusses unusually active speculation in South Sea Company shares, recording successive quoted figures of 177 and 184, plus a forecast that prices could climb to 200. These are newspaper price claims rather than verified individual purchases.

reported_numbers.meaning: Earlier South Sea share quotation as reported
Price expected by unnamed market participants, not a realized price

limitations: Original Dutch spelling not independently transcribed in this dataset. Yale's translation is not reproduced verbatim. News dates, quotation basis and settlement prices require checking against original editions and exchange ledgers.

title: Dutch Paris dispatch reports halted cash redemption and alleged opposition
paraphrase: The French dispatch reports a halt in cash payments for bank bills the preceding day and fears about depletion of the bank's treasury. It also relays suspicion that people were deliberately undermining the bank: this is a contemporaneous rumor, not established wrongdoing. A separate passage describes expensive food and restrictions on animal slaughter.
limitations: Reporting of rumored deliberate obstruction is not independent evidence of a plot. Yale's 22 April newspaper reference is a report/edition date as presented by Yale; the French administrative order must be checked independently for precise legal and implementation chronology.

title: Dutch paper reproduces London committee account of unauthorized share schemes
place: London dispatch appearing in Dutch-language newspaper
paraphrase: A London-dated dispatch says a parliamentary committee believed it had found 70 dubious promotional projects and expected legislation to suppress them. This is a contemporary report of claims about parliamentary intentions, not proof each of the purported 70 was illegal or eventually closed.

reported_numbers.meaning: Contemporary newspaper assertion about committee findings, not audited enacted closures

limitations: 14 June is the date in the London dispatch, not independently the Dutch issue publication date. Original visible in Yale's clipping, modern English translation used as guide. No verified international news transit duration.

title: A historical reading of enslaved populations in 1721 New Orleans and vicinity
paraphrase: Historian J. Hanno Deiler reproduces figures attributed to Diron's November 1721 census: 177 people classified as African and held in slavery, 21 Indigenous people held in slavery, and 28 European contracted laborers (engagés). These are categories recorded or repeated by colonial observers, not natural identities or comprehensive community histories.

reported_numbers.meaning: African-descended people recorded as enslaved, historical reproduction only
Indigenous people recorded as enslaved, historical reproduction only
European laborers classified as engagés, historical reproduction only

limitations: Reproduced in 1910, not independently verified against 1721 handwritten folios. Scope is New Orleans and nearby areas, not all Louisiana. Spellings and exact categories may differ; some people were omitted or anonymized. The figures should not be combined into an overall population total until definitions and other publications are reconciled.

title: 1917 historian reports different population summary from the 1721 census
place: New Orleans (town; excludes some outlying concessions)
paraphrase: Historian Marc de Villiers du Terrage's historical account presents a New Orleans total of 470 inhabitants with 277 Europeans from a November 24, 1721 census. The work also gives separate figures for surrounding settlements; its digitized table contains imperfect text extraction.

reported_numbers.meaning: Author's summary count for New Orleans town
Europeans within the author's town count

limitations: Figures and geographic boundaries must be verified against original census. Different published transcriptions may partition town, concessions, households, or statuses differently; do not add separate enslaved figures from another edition to infer a shared denominator.

title: 1735 Louisiana card-money ceiling in an 1892 reproduction of a royal ordinance
paraphrase: Zay's 1892 publication reproduces a September 1735 royal ordinance: article I prescribes fabrication of card money up to a 200,000-livre nominal ceiling; article IV requires four registers/records for each fabrication; article V forbids officials to authorize a higher sum; article VI provides for circulation and acceptance at royal stores and for bills of exchange. The preamble claims Crown specie sent after the 1731 retrocession flowed back to France. These are stated legal provisions and royal claims, not audited money movements, actual card issuance, creditor settlements, or evidence that Indigenous nations or enslaved people consented.

reported_numbers.meaning: Maximum nominal card-money fabrication authorized by the 1735 text as reprinted in 1892; not verified issued, paid, redeemed, or transferred to Company creditors

limitations: Original 1735 royal ordinance and official register/folio were not inspected. This is a historical reprint read via digitized text extraction; BnF-derived mirror OCR renders the heading '260 m.' while the Wikimedia OCR and repeated articles I, IV, V read '200 m.'. The 1892 and BnF-derived scans are not independent eighteenth-century witnesses. Confirm printed image and original law before asserting textual variants or any observed circulation.

title: HNOC catalogue abstract mentions Macmahon sale of people enslaved by Company
paraphrase: The Historic New Orleans Collection's Surrey Calendar abstract for a two-page ministerial letter dated 2 September 1732 (Marly; Minister of Marine to Salmon; ANOM B57:815) lists Macmahon's sale of people enslaved by the Company and separately lists approval of a Superior Council decision in the Diron–Company of the Indies case. The abstract does not say that these two subjects were connected. Its historical racialized term is not adopted here as a description of the people.
limitations: Only the HNOC catalogue abstract was read; the two-page original letter was not examined. 2 September 1732 is the letter date, not a proven date of sale. The abstract supplies no names, number, purchaser, price, receipt, payment, transfer terms or legal basis. It does not connect the sale subject to the Diron decision or the 24 February 1731 debt decree. This is an imperial administrative summary and preserves no voice or consent of the enslaved people. Do not infer their identities or community affiliation from the catalogue wording.

title: Company creditor claims preserved in a contemporary periodical extract of the 23 January 1731 retrocession decree
paraphrase: The March 1731 Mercure de France text places an entry headed “AUTRE du même jour, concernant la rétrocession...” immediately after an item dated 23 January. Its pp. 610–611 extract reports that the King accepted the Company's retrocession of the Louisiana and Illinois concession and exclusive-trade privilege, declared Louisiana commerce free to all his subjects, and preserved the Company's rights against its debtors in the province. The OCR transcription reads: “Maintient, S.M. ladite Compagnie dans les droits qu'elle a contre ses débiteurs de ladite Province” (p. 611). This is a Company-side creditor claim/receivable right; it is not evidence of a Company liability or of Crown assumption of the Company's debts.
limitations: Only the Bureau du Mercure OCR transcription was read; the March 1731 periodical page image, original royal printing and ANOM COL F3 242 fol.187 were not examined. The original royal decree was not examined. The portal describes its contents as exploratory, provisional and incomplete, so OCR errors and omissions remain possible. This is a contemporary periodical extract, not a diplomatic transcription of the complete royal decree. It is not the separate 24 February 1731 decree concerning payment of the Company's Louisiana debts. The extract names no debtor, amount, lawsuit, collection, receipt or payment and does not prove that any Company claim was enforced. It is a French royal/Company legal perspective and records neither Indigenous consent to territorial claims nor the experiences of enslaved people.

title: Choctaw-negotiated Youanis post and unresolved identity of the 1732 'Youanis (Yazoo)' exception
place: Haiyow ni / Youani / Éiouanné, southern Choctaw country
paraphrase: Musco, Ellis and Spring, Gradhiva 40 (2025), pp.101–106, reconstruct the Choctaw-requested Youanis post from colonial archival citations. They cite ANOM C13A 1721 fol.146 for the Choctaw request accepted on 8 February 1721; C13A 1725a fol.65v and 1725b fol.129v for renewed requests; C13A 1726 fol.159 for Merveilleux's first mention of Haiyow ni (Youani/Éiouanné) as a possible site; C13A 1729d fols.31–31v for the Choctaw delegation and negotiations in which chiefs chose a trading store in their territory and negotiated prices; and C13A 1733 fol.202 for construction in February–March 1730 under Régis du Roullet. The authors interpret these negotiations as evidence that Choctaw leaders exercised political authority and controlled important terms of French settlement; they also report that French officials asked the chiefs to help protect the soldiers at the post. Ryan Spring is a co-author and Cultural Research Associate with the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma. Separately, HNOC's abstract for Salmon's 19 January 1732 letter lists an exception called 'Youanis (Yazoo)'. The article does not identify that exception as the Haiyow ni/Youanis post; identity remains unresolved.
limitations: This is an English-language scholarly synthesis, not a transcription of the cited French archival folios; ANOM C13A fols.146, 65v, 129v, 159, 31–31v and 202 were not directly examined in this atlas. The authors' account of Choctaw agency is scholarly interpretation grounded in colonial records and Indigenous historical expertise, not a verbatim Choctaw oral testimony. The HNOC original two-page letter ANOM C13 15:31 was not examined; 'Youanis (Yazoo)' is the HNOC catalogue abstract's wording and is not verified as wording in Salmon's letter. Shared spelling does not establish same-site identity, asset transfer, reason for exception, or coordinates. The Gradhiva figure caption dates a Dumont de Montigny map 1736; Archives nationales' 2026 caption gives 1746 for the map at the same old cote, while Versailles' 2025 press kit says 'after 1736'. The map itself and its full archival record were not examined, so the map date remains unresolved. The English translation of the article reports the Diron award as '29,000 pounds' (p.105); the original French wording and cited ANOM C13A 1732 fols.33–33v were not examined, so the atlas's French-livre normalization remains provisional. The award is not evidence of payment.

title: Scholarly cross-check of the 1731 Superior Council reorganization and unresolved 22/24 May references
paraphrase: Khalil Saadani, “Le Gouvernement de la Louisiane Française, 1731–43,” French Colonial History 4 (2003), pp. 117–118, describes the Company's withdrawal as simplifying Louisiana's administrative structure: the Conseil de régie that represented the Company disappeared; royal letters patent dated 22 May 1731 restored the Conseil supérieur according to the 1716 edict and revoked the August 1719 provisions that had required some Company directors to sit on it. Saadani says the formal administrative link to Canada resumed, while noting that distance made it largely theoretical and that Louisiana officials continued direct correspondence with the minister. Saadani's note 3 (p. 131) also cites AN, Archives de la Marine A1-69 fol. 20 as letters patent dated 24 May 1731, alongside AN, Colonies A22 fols. 134–135, A23 fols. 106–107, B55 fols. 634–635, and C13A13 fol. 260 (a draft). Separately, Alexandre Ribeaux (2026), PDF p. 8 n. 39, identifies a copy of an edict dated 22 May 1731 at ANOM COL F3 242 fol. 190 and says Company directors were excluded from the Superior Council; he notes that the cited text does not mention judges in distant places. The 22 May F3 242 copy and Saadani's 24 May A1-69 reference may be related copies, separate instruments, or a citation/date discrepancy; their relationship is unresolved. These are scholarly readings and archival locators, not a transcription of either original. The sources identify a category of Company directors excluded from the Council but do not name an individual roster.
limitations: The cited ANOM/Archives nationales folios (COL F3 242 fol. 190; A1-69 fol. 20; A22 fols. 134–135; A23 fols. 106–107; B55 fols. 634–635; C13A13 fol. 260) were not directly examined. Saadani's article is a secondary synthesis; Ribeaux's footnote is a secondary archival citation. The 22 May and 24 May references are not reconciled and must not be silently merged. No named Company directors, appointment roster, individual vote, detailed implementation, continued status of judges in remote posts, Company property transfer, corporate debt assumption, liability, settlement, amount or payment is established here. The monetary-indemnity claim elsewhere in Saadani's article is deliberately not imported into this extract. This is a Crown/Company administrative perspective, not evidence of Indigenous consent or a transfer of Choctaw sovereignty. Choctaw Nation's Iti Fabvssa account describes Choctaw-led diplomacy and the important role of women in negotiations, but it does not discuss this 1731 edict; it is contextual community-authored history, not a direct response to this instrument. Original folios were not examined; this is scholarly interpretation, not a transcription.

title: Full three-page transcription of the 23 January 1731 Louisiana retrocession decree
place: Marly (Council of State); Louisiana and the Illinois country (territories named)
paraphrase: The 1731 printed royal decree, read from a 1985 CIHM/ICMH microfiche reproduction of a Seminary of Quebec Library copy, records the Company's retrocession through its syndics and directors. The King accepts the return of the property, seigneurie and justice of Louisiana and its dependencies and the country of the Illinois, along with the places, forts, buildings, artillery, arms and troops then present. The King also accepts the return of the Company's exclusive-trade privilege and declares Louisiana commerce free to all his subjects. The final operative passage expressly maintains the Company's rights against its debtors in the province, exercisable when and as the Company judges appropriate. The preceding phrase that the Company is not to be charged in future follows the return of the exclusive-trade privilege; reading it as a general discharge of the Company's separate debts would go beyond this text. The decree names no debtor, amount, collection, receipt or payment.

transcription_pages.text:
ARREST DU CONSEIL D’ESTAT DU ROY,
Concernant la rétrocession faite à Sa Majesté par la Compagnie des Indes, de la concession de la Louisiane & du pays des Illinois.
Du 23. Janvier 1731.
Extrait des Registres du Conseil d’Estat.

SUR la Requeste présentée au Roy par les Directeurs & Syndics de la Compagnie des Indes, à ce dûment authorisez par délibération de ladite Compagnie du 22. Janvier

dernier, tendante à ce qu’il plût à Sa Majesté accepter la rétrocession de la concession de la Province de la Louisiane, & du pays des Sauvages Illinois, pour estre réunis & incorporez à son Domaine, ensemble la rétrocession du privilege exclusif du commerce de ladite Colonie, en le déclarant libre à tous ses Sujets; à quoy, désirant pourvoir.

Oüy le Rapport du Sieur Orry Conseiller d’Estat, & ordinaire au Conseil Royal, Contrôleur general des Finances, SA MAJESTÉ ESTANT EN SON CONSEIL; a accepté & accepte la rétrocession à Elle faite par les Syndics & Directeurs de la Compagnie des Indes, pour, & au nom de ladite Compagnie, de la propriété, Seigneurie & Justice de la Province de la Louisiane; & de toutes ses dépendances, ensemble du pays des Sauvages Illinois, laquelle concession luy avoit esté accordée à temps ou à perpetuité, par les Edits & Arrests des mois d’Aoust & Septembre 1717. May 1719. Juillet 1720, & Juin 1725; pour estre ladite Province réunie au Domaine de Sa Majesté; ensemble de toutes les Places, Forts, Bastimens, Artillerie; Armemens, & Troupes qui y sont actuellement. Accepte pareillement la rétrocession du privilege du commerce exclusif que ladite Compagnie faisoit dans cette concession; au

moyen de quoy Sa Majesté declare le commerce de la Louisiane libre à tous ses Sujets, sans que la Compagnie en puisse estre chargée à l’avenir, sous quelque pretexte que ce soit : Maintient, Sa Majesté, ladite Compagnie dans les droits qu’elle a contre ses debiteurs de ladite Province ; qu’elle luy permet d’exercer quand & comme elle le jugera à propos. Et seront pour l’execution du present Arrest toutes Lettres necessaires expediées.

FAIT au Conseil d’Estat du Roy, Sa Majesté y estant, tenu à Marly le vingt-troisieme Janvier mil sept cens trente-un. Signé PHELYPEAUX.

A PARIS ;
DE L’IMPRIMERIE ROYALE,
M. DCCXXXI.

limitations: The printed text was visually transcribed from the three page images in a 1985 CIHM/ICMH 22X microfiche reproduction; the microfiche front matter identifies the Seminary of Quebec Library as the source of the filmed copy and notes discoloured/show-through pages. The physical 1731 copy and ANOM COL F3 242 fol. 187 were not examined. The transcription is checked against the facsimile images and extracted OCR but is not a diplomatic transcription made by the holding library; punctuation and long-s spellings should be checked against a higher-resolution copy before critical edition use. The March 1731 Mercure de France extract (pp. 610–611) is a separate contemporary periodical abridgement/OCR and has not been collated against its page image here. This is not the separate 24 February 1731 Company-debt decree, whose operative clauses remain unread. The instrument speaks from the French Crown/Company perspective and does not record Indigenous consent; the Peoria Tribe's community-authored history is contextual and does not claim to respond to this decree. The decree does not identify enslaved people or prove that people were among the listed material assets. No debtor, amount, enforcement, collection, receipt, payment, settlement or Crown assumption of Company liabilities is established.

title: Duval succession account balance reported by an English index card; manuscript account unread
place: New Orleans, French Louisiana (archive collection context)
paraphrase: The first browser-accessible image for Louisiana Historical Center record 1732-07-15-01 is an English typed index card numbered #6558. Its heading reads “STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS DUE FROM THE IND. CO.” The prose says it closes the account of François Duval, former cashier-general of the India Company, with that Company as of 15 January 1736, and reports a balance due the Company by the succession of Sr. Duval of 101,975 livres 6 sols 2 deniers. The card says the statement was signed on 15 July 1732 by Bruslé and on 15 January 1736 by Prévost. The heading suggests a different direction of debt from the prose. The four handwritten manuscript-page image derivatives were opened but not reliably transcribed. The catalogue date, account-as-of date and sign-off dates remain unreconciled.
transcription:
#6558
YEAR 1732 JULY 15
STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS DUE FROM THE IND. CO.
Statement showing closing of account of Sr. Francois Duval, former Cashier-General of the India Company, with said Company as of 15 January 1736, showing a balance due the company by the Succession of Sr. Duval, of 101,975 livres 6 sols 2 deniers.
(Signed) On July 15, 1732, by Bruslé.
On January 15, 1736, by Prevost.
Not printed in Louisiana Historical Quarterly.

reported_numbers.meaning: The card's composite wording is 101,975 livres 6 sols 2 deniers; the subunits are separately preserved below and the handwritten account was not transcribed.

reported_amounts.direction_in_prose: balance due the Company by the succession of Sr. Duval

limitations: Only the typed English index card and four browser-accessible 800x0 manuscript image derivatives were visually examined. The card is not the original account; its author/date and its specific relationship to the WPA abstracts are not established. The LHC project says its initial index used WPA summaries from 1935–1942 and warns that those abstracts contain errors and omit many enslaved people's and women's names; this general method does not prove this particular card is a WPA abstract. The record page labels the item 15 July 1732, while the card gives an account-as-of date and second sign-off on 15 January 1736. The heading and prose conflict about debt direction. The reported balance is not a verified liability, receivable, settlement or payment. No relation to the 24 February 1731 decree is established. The card records only a colonial Company/accounting perspective and cannot stand in for Indigenous or enslaved people's experiences or consent.

title: Index card #6022 reports a 1736 receipt involving Jean Labbe, Guillon and a Company debt; manuscript unread
place: New Orleans, Province of Louisiana (archive record context)
paraphrase: The Louisiana Historical Center dates record 1736-08-20-04 to 20 August 1736 and categorizes it as a private receipt. Its first displayed image is typed English index card #6022. The card says a receipt to Jean Labbe concerned the price of a person the card calls “negro,” sold to Guillon, and that this formed part of the 5,845 livres for which Labe was indebted to the Company. This is an index-card report, not a transcription of the two handwritten pages. The 5,845 livres is reported indebtedness, not a verified balance or payment; the card does not establish whether the sale proceeds were received or credited to the Company.
transcription:
#6022
YEAR 1736 AUGUST 20
Receipt to Jean Labbe for price of negro sold to Guillon, which was part of the 5845 livres for which Labe was indebted to the Company.

Listed in Louisiana Historical Quarterly, Vol. 8, No. 3, P. 489- 2nd Doc. July 1925.

reported_numbers.meaning: The English index card says Labe was indebted to the Company for 5845 livres and says the sale price formed part of that amount. This is not a verified account balance, sale price, amount received, payment or settlement.

limitations: Only typed English index card #6022 was transcribed. Two handwritten page derivatives were opened but not reliably transcribed; the 600 dpi preservation TIFF masters were not accessed. The card's author/date and relationship to WPA summaries are unverified. The record-page date is not proven to be the date of the underlying sale or payment. The card does not state a separate sale price, identify the enslaved person, specify a payer/payee, or prove that proceeds were remitted to or credited by the Company. The 5845 livres is a card-reported debt, not a verified balance or payment. The LHC inventory confirms Louisiana Historical Quarterly vol. 8 no. 3 (July 1925) exists, but p. 489 was not examined. The card's historical terminology and colonial account perspective do not convey the enslaved person's voice; the LHC warns that WPA-era abstracts omit many enslaved people's and women's names, but this specific card is not proven to be WPA-derived. No connection to the 24 February 1731 decree is established.

title: Catalogue description of Salmon's 14 August 1734 letter on Company house-advance claims and requested half remission
place: New Orleans (as stated in item metadata)
paraphrase: Archives de la Nouvelle-France item 31196 identifies a ten-image French letter from Salmon to the minister, dated 14 August 1734 and responding to a dispatch of 16 February 1734. The catalogue describes Company claims against Louisiana inhabitants and concessionnaires for repayment of advances for houses and says Salmon requested remission of half the debts because of insolvency attributed to bad years. This is a transcription/paraphrase of the catalogue description only; the ten archival images have not been examined. Saadani (2008, printed pp.27–29) places Company-colonist debt disputes and reduction proposals in the wider post-retrocession context, but the accessible excerpt does not establish a direct documentary link to the 1734 letter or HNOC item 8981.
transcription: Catalogue wording fragments only: “Lettre de Salmon au ministre en réponse à sa dépêche du 16 février 1734.” The item summary also says: “Salmon demande la remise de la moitié des dettes.” These are catalogue phrases, not a transcription of the letter.
limitations: The source is an archival portal item record, not the ten-page letter. Its summary does not establish individual debts, amounts, ministerial decision, approved remission, collection, payment, settlement or Crown assumption. The catalogue's wording about house advances must be checked against the original French. The 1734 letter is not proven to be the same correspondence as HNOC item 8981 or the 30 March 1735 ordinance, and no explicit cross-reference to the 24 February 1731 decree has been established. Saadani is a secondary synthesis; accessible preview pp.27–29 does not include the cited notes 33–46. This colonial administrative description does not preserve the experiences of inhabitants, enslaved people or Indigenous nations; pair it with judicial petitions and community-authored histories rather than treating the ledger's categories as a complete social account.

title: Company register extracts record a 1,450,000-livre undertaking after the King reduced a 3,600,000-livre estimate; 24 January 1731
place: Company assembly location not stated; the quoted ministerial message is dated Marly, 22 January 1731
paraphrase: The Louisiana Historical Center's 24-page item 1731-01-24-03 contains an 1889 certified archival copy of extracts from Company of the Indies administrative registers. The copied heading identifies an extract of the Company's general assembly register dated 22 January 1731 and a separate heading for deliberations of the Company's general and particular committees on 24 January 1731. The latter records a royal message relayed from Marly on 22 January: the Secretary of State for the Marine estimated an equivalent at 3,600,000 livres, but the King reduced and fixed it at 1,450,000 livres, scheduled over ten years (200,000 in each of the first three years, 150,000 in each of the next three, and 100,000 in each of the final four). The Company assembly authorized its syndics and directors to submit, for the Company, an undertaking to pay the 1,450,000-livre amount under those terms, subject to a further royal order and prescribed form. This is a Company-to-Crown undertaking candidate, not proof of formal execution or payment. The preceding Company petition also describes an alternative under which the Company would retain exclusive trade while supplying 500 enslaved people per year; that is a proposed condition, not an actual shipment.

transcription_pages.text: Heading identifies an extract from the Company's general register of deliberations in general administrative assemblies, dated 22 January 1731; the copy is filed under Ministry of Marine and Colonies / Company of the Indies cartons.

The Company's alternative proposal refers to 'cinq cent nègres par an' (five hundred enslaved people per year) as a proposed supply condition if the Company retained exclusive trade; not evidence of actual shipments.

Heading: 'Délibérations prises dans les Comités Généraux et particuliers du 24 Janvier 1731.' The page records the meeting of the Company's syndics and directors and reads a letter from the Controller General dated Marly, 22 January 1731.

The royal message describes 'Trois millions six cent mille livres' as the Secretary of State's estimate and says the King reduced the sum to 'Quatorze cent cinquante mille livres seulement'. It gives a ten-year schedule: 200,000 livres in each of the first three years, 150,000 in each of the next three, and 100,000 in each of the final four.

The Company assembly authorized the syndics and directors to make, on behalf of the Company, 'leur soumission de payer la susdite somme' (their undertaking to pay the stated sum), subject to the King's order and prescribed form.

The archive certification, dated Paris, 20 September 1889, states that the extracts conform to a collated copy deposited in the archives; this identifies the surviving witness as a certified archival copy, not the original 1731 register.
A second ministerial certification dated 20 September 1889 authenticates the archive official's signature; no payment receipt or treasury account appears on this certification page.

reported_numbers.meaning: Secretary of State for the Marine's estimate of the equivalent in the quoted royal message; not the final amount fixed by the King.
Amount fixed by the King in the quoted message and the amount the Company assembly authorized its directors to submit to pay; no actual payment is verified.
Scheduled for each of the first three years of the ten-year undertaking; not proof of installment payment.
Scheduled for each of the next three years; not proof of installment payment.
Scheduled for each of the final four years; not proof of installment payment.
Alternative proposed condition for retaining exclusive trade; not an actual shipment or population count.

limitations: This is a transcription of selected legible phrases and a paraphrase from 800px image derivatives of an 1889 certified copy; the original 1731 Company register and 600dpi preservation TIFFs were not examined. Only 24 of 48 image links were inspected. The LHC catalogue's 'French Superior Council' source label conflicts with the internal Ministry of Marine / Company-cartons heading. The four attached English typed summary cards are derivative; the exact crosswalk to WPA Black Book 20 is unverified, and their summary omits the reduction from 3,600,000 to 1,450,000 livres. The 1,450,000-livre figure is a Company-authorized submission subject to further royal order/form, not proof of a final instrument, legal adjudication, receipt or payment. No treasury accounts or installment receipts were examined. The proposed 500 enslaved people per year is not an actual shipment. The Company petition's description of the Natchez conflict is a corporate colonial perspective; it does not represent Natchez political perspectives or establish that Natchez people ceased to exist. The Natchez Nation's official contemporary self-description and NPS historical context are included separately. This record is distinct from the 24 February 1731 Company-debt decree; no direct cross-reference is established.
